Embryonic development in the Devils River minnow proceeds rapidly under controlled laboratory conditions. At a constant temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], most embryos successfully hatch after just 5 days , a relatively brief incubation period characteristic of small-bodied cyprinids adapted to warm, spring-fed headwaters. Following hatch, the prolarvae remain in a non-feeding, yolk-dependent state for approximately 8 days before transitioning to first exogenous feeding. Field biologists typically express the total length at birth as a range reflecting this early developmental plasticity, with Day-8 mesolarvae measuring between 0.58 and 0.84 centimeters (0.58-0.84 centimeters) [Lb = 0.58-0.84 centimeters] after conversion from standard length. During this lecithotrophic phase, the wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.0021 grams [Wwb = 0.0021 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of 1.6 millimeters reported in earlier literature. This minimal neonatal mass underscores the energetic constraints faced by larvae emerging into a resource-limited spring environment where the onset of exotrophic feeding is critical for survival.

Despite their diminutive starting size, individuals of Dionda diaboli can ultimately attain a much larger adult body size. The maximum recorded total length for this species is 6.4 centimeters [Li = 6.4 centimeters], a figure that places it among the middle-sized members of its genus. Correlating with this ultimate length, the theoretical adult wet weight, representing the mass of a fully-grown adult, is estimated at approximately 2.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.2 grams], a value derived from a length-weight regression. This represents a thousand-fold increase from the approximately 0.0021 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0021 grams] at hatching, highlighting the substantial growth trajectory required to reach reproductive size. The transition to sexual maturity occurs well before this maximum size is reached, however. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonad maturation and the commencement of gametogenesis, occurs when individuals attain a total length ranging from 2.5 to 0.84 centimeters (2.5-0.84 centimeters) [Lp = 2.5-0.84 centimeters], a rather broad interval that may reflect considerable variation in individual growth rates and local resource availability within their spring and creek habitats.

Under constant thermal conditions of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], the age at hatching and subsequent development to the free-swimming larval stage have been closely monitored in captive rearing trials. The age at birth, defined as the period post-hatch, is 13 days [ab = 13 days], which includes the incubation period of 5 days  and an additional 8 days of yolk-sac absorption before the onset of active feeding at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C] at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. This comparatively short developmental window is an adaptation to the thermally stable but resource-poor spring habitats the species occupies. Regarding the species' ultimate longevity, the maximum lifespan in captivity has been documented at 730 days [am = 730 days] at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. This lifespan, just over two years, is typical for a small cyprinid with an annual reproductive strategy, though it may be truncated in the wild by predation and environmental fluctuations, meaning the realized ecological lifespan is often considerably shorter than this physiological maximum.

Reproductive output in the Devils River minnow reflects its status as an iteroparous, multiple-batch spawner. At a water temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], a single gravid female can release an average of 100 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 100 eggs per spawning event]. Given the extended spawning period that can last several months under optimal conditions, an individual female may complete approximately 1 clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch of eggs each year], though this frequency can vary with water temperature and food availability. The maximum reproductive rate, determined from size-corrected estimates derived from the related European minnow Phoxinus phoxinus, suggests moderate fecundity when scaled to the species' ultimate total length of 6.4 centimeters [Li = 6.4 centimeters]. This relatively modest per-event output is common among small-bodied stream fishes that invest in producing a small number of large, well-yolked eggs, which in turn enhances larval survival in the clear, low-productivity waters of the Edwards Plateau.

Habitat degradation and the introduction of non-native fishes have significantly impacted populations of Dionda diaboli across its limited range in the Rio Grande drainage. The species is now listed as threatened under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, prompting considerable research into its life history to inform recovery efforts. One key parameter for population viability models is the onset of sexual maturation, which field surveys indicate can occur across a wide interval of 2.5 to 0.84 centimeters (2.5-0.84 centimeters) [Lp = 2.5-0.84 centimeters], a substantial range that may reflect compensatory responses to high mortality. Furthermore, the allometric relationship between length and mass yields a predicted asymptotic adult weight of approximately 2.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.2 grams]. Understanding these metrics, from the 5 days  required for egg hatching at 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C] to the 730 days [am = 730 days] maximum lifespan, is fundamental for constructing effective conservation strategies that prioritize the preservation of the cool, clean spring flows upon which this endemic minnow depends.
